_comment: WA-Chain's own verified research, used by the consultation assistant as a second source after the course material. Each topic becomes one citable document and each fact one block, so an answer can point at the exact fact. Only conclusions that passed WA-Chain's fact-checks go here, written in our own words (never transcribed from a book). `sources` are shown to the reader next to the citation. `checked` names the WA-Chain record the fact comes from (kept in the WA-Chain folder, not in this repo). Add a fact by appending to a topic; keep ids stable.

topics.title: Fibre dimensions and identification of kōzo, gampi and mitsumata

facts.title: Fibre length
facts.text: Kōzo has by far the longest fibre of the three: a peer-reviewed survey gives 6–21 mm with an average of about 9.4 mm, and other institutional sources give roughly 10–15 mm. Gampi and mitsumata both run about 3 mm (reported range 3–5 mm). Wood pulp for comparison is about 1–3 mm. Agreement across independent sources is high. WA-Chain does not use separate average values for gampi and mitsumata beyond 'about 3 mm', because their individual averages were not confirmed by a second source.

facts.title: Fibre width does not separate the three
facts.text: Reported fibre widths of kōzo, gampi and mitsumata overlap, roughly within 10–30 micrometres, so width alone cannot identify the fibre. An apparent conflict in the literature over mitsumata (about 12 µm in one source, about 20 µm in another) was resolved by WA-Chain: the average is about 9–12 µm and about 20 µm is the upper end of the range, not an average. Several reference atlases may share one original source, so their agreement is not fully independent.

facts.title: Kōzo is easy to identify; gampi and mitsumata are easily confused
facts.text: Cellulose composition is nearly the same in all three fibres, so chemical identification depends on residual lignin and then hemicellulose. In one peer-reviewed feasibility study, kōzo was identified without error, while gampi and mitsumata, both of the Thymelaeaceae family, were easily confused with each other. This is a single small study and should be presented as such. Separately, kōzo paper beaten to a gloss can be mistaken for gampi by eye.

facts.title: The plants
facts.text: Kōzo belongs to the mulberry family (Moraceae) and is cultivated; cut stumps send up new shoots whose bark is the raw material. Mitsumata and gampi belong to the Thymelaeaceae (the daphne family). Of the three, it is gampi that is gathered from the wild because it is hard to cultivate, which makes gampi paper expensive. The wild-only point is made for gampi alone; the sources do not say it of mitsumata.

topics.title: Chemistry, pH and permanence of washi, with corrections to common claims

facts.title: Measured pH
facts.text: Traditionally made washi is close to neutral or mildly alkaline. Measured values: kōzo paper pH 6.3–9.5; mitsumata and gampi paper pH 6.6–8.6. The alkalinity comes largely from alkali left by cooking the fibre, which is why washi is valued as acid-free in Western conservation. Several independent sources agree.

sources.label: AIC Book and Paper Group Annual (Murphy & Rempel 1985, measured values)
IFLA: Paper conservation by using Japanese paper (washi)

facts.checked: 三原料比較_統合ソース評価_最終_2026-07

facts.title: Correction: gampi paper is not acidic
facts.text: A Japanese conservation reference states that gampi paper tends to be acidic. WA-Chain found no independent support for this: measured values put gampi and mitsumata paper at pH 6.6–8.6, neutral to mildly alkaline. WA-Chain therefore does not use the claim, and where it is mentioned, notes that independent measurement points the other way.

facts.title: Yellowing and embrittlement have different main causes
facts.text: Low lignin does make washi less prone to yellowing. But mechanical deterioration (embrittlement) is governed mainly by acidity rather than lignin content: at neutral pH, lignin content made no significant difference to the rate of degradation, loss of degree of polymerisation tracks acidity, and the historic poor durability of paper traced back to acidification from aluminium sulphate. WA-Chain presents this in two layers: yellowing relates to lignin, embrittlement to acidity.

facts.title: Hemicellulose and wet strength
facts.text: In a controlled experiment on kōzo (Broussonetia kazinoki), adding hemicellulose (glucuronoxylan) raised wet tensile strength in proportion to the amount added, a causal result. By contrast, the claim that gampi and mitsumata contain more hemicellulose than kōzo was not supported by independent checking; composition of the three is broadly similar, so WA-Chain avoids ranking them on this.

sources.label: Han et al. 2023, Molecules (peer-reviewed, controlled experiment)

topics.title: What is not established about the three fibres

facts.title: No measured strength ranking of the three
facts.text: Simple strength rankings such as 'kōzo strongest, mitsumata weaker, gampi weakest' were not supported when WA-Chain checked them. Statements that mitsumata is the weakest circulate in paper dealers' descriptions, which are not measurement data. WA-Chain found no study measuring the tensile or folding strength of kōzo, mitsumata and gampi papers under the same conditions. What can be said is that kōzo's long fibre makes strong paper even when thin.

sources.label: WA-Chain literature search, July 2026

facts.title: Gampi and insects: a candidate mechanism, not a proven one
facts.text: The claim that gampi paper attracts fewer insects is traditional and anecdotal. Plants of the gampi genus (Wikstroemia, Thymelaeaceae) contain compounds with reported insecticidal or toxic activity, such as daphnane diterpenoids and coumarins. But this is the chemistry of the living plant; WA-Chain found no study showing that these compounds survive alkaline cooking and washing to give the finished paper any insect resistance. It should not be used as a selection criterion.

topics.title: How each fibre is used in conservation

facts.title: Kōzo
facts.text: Kōzo papers are the mainstay of lining in Japanese mounting: thin Mino paper (usumino) for the first lining, Misu paper (with shell white) and Uda paper (with white clay) for later linings, and kōzo strips for fold reinforcement.

facts.title: Gampi
facts.text: Gampi paper is used for the final backing of handscrolls, and in maniai paper (gampi with mud, made by the tame-zuki method) and torinoko paper.

facts.title: Mitsumata: role in conservation is thinly documented
facts.text: WA-Chain found no reliable source for a use specific to mitsumata alone in Japanese mounting, and the claim that mitsumata is widely used for infills was not supported. A professional conference postprint notes that gampi and mitsumata papers are used less often than kōzo in objects conservation. Reported practice includes kōzo–mitsumata blend tissues (for example Berlin Tissue, used as a remoistenable tissue) and choosing mitsumata for a tone close to aged paper, but these reports are secondary. One documented museum case uses a mitsumata paper for infill: see the Metropolitan Museum herbal case.

topics.title: Kōzo provenance: species and growing regions

facts.title: Kōzo is not a single plant
facts.text: Cultivated kōzo in Japan is generally a hybrid of hime-kōzo and kajinoki (Broussonetia × kazinoki). The kōzo imported from Thailand is kajinoki (Broussonetia papyrifera) alone. This is general botanical classification and should be confirmed in a flora for strict use. Fibre figures such as 6–21 mm length are for kōzo as a raw material; WA-Chain found no reliable region-by-region fibre measurements.

facts.checked: 楮の産地別情報まとめ

facts.title: Nasu kōzo (Daigo, Ibaraki)
facts.text: Nasu kōzo is grown mainly in Daigo town, Ibaraki, and along the Tochigi–Fukushima border; the name comes from its trade route. Hon-Mino paper and Echizen hōsho are made only from Daigo Nasu kōzo. The town reports its use in conservation of cultural property abroad and in printmaking paper, and describes production as critically low.

facts.title: Sekishū kōzo (Iwami, Shimane)
facts.text: Sekishū banshi is known above all for its strength, attributed to a process that keeps the amakawa, the green layer just under the outer bark. It is made by nagashi-zuki from local kōzo grown for three years. An Edo-period agricultural text describes the 'makōzo' grown in Iwami as having soft, long, strong and lustrous fibre of the best quality. Sekishū banshi was designated an Important Intangible Cultural Property in 1969 and is part of UNESCO's 'Washi, craftsmanship of traditional Japanese hand-made paper' (2014, extending the 2009 listing).

facts.title: Tosa kōzo (Niyodo river, Kōchi)
facts.text: Tosa tengujō is made from local kōzo of the Niyodo river basin and is extremely thin yet strong, called 'mayfly wings'. One maker supplies tengujō for cultural-property conservation at 2.0 g/m², described as the thinnest in the world. Kōchi was Japan's largest washi-producing region from the end of the Edo period to the early Shōwa period.

facts.text: Domestic kōzo fell to about 15% over some thirty years, and Thai kōzo became more than half of the main raw material (figures from a 2017 study). topics.title: Washi in Western conservation: documented museum cases

facts.title: Why washi is chosen
facts.text: Washi is a first-choice repair material in Western paper conservation because its long kōzo fibre is strong even when thin, it is neutral to mildly alkaline, and bonded with wheat starch paste it can be released with water, keeping the treatment reversible. The cases below are summaries of each institution's published treatment records; WA-Chain has not independently verified them.

facts.title: Chester Beatty Library: the Coëtivy Hours (guarding and mounting)
facts.text: The Coëtivy Hours (French, c. 1443, on parchment, CBL W 082): 144 of its 148 three-quarter-page miniatures had been cut out and held between glass, and were re-mounted for digitisation and safe handling. The conservator used two kōzo papers for two jobs: two 25 mm tabs of the stronger sekishū on the spine edge to hold it securely, and three to five 15 mm tabs of the lighter usumino on the other three edges to leave the parchment room to expand and contract. On folio 295, four damaged areas along the spine were repaired with a sekishū dyed with yasha (alder cones) at 20 g/m², chosen thinner and lighter than the parchment to avoid tension. Wheat starch paste throughout. The weights of the tab papers are not stated in the record.

facts.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Grüninger's Gart der Gesuntheit (mending and infill)
facts.text: Der Gart der Gesuntheit, printed by Johann Grüninger in Strasbourg c. 1489 (378 woodcuts, 26 gatherings, Met 44.7.21), was one of the most damaged of 186 volumes treated under a New York State conservation grant: water damage, insect holes, and coarse earlier repairs that limited opening to 45 degrees. After removing old repairs with wheat starch paste poultices, losses were first stabilised with a thin kōzo paper (Akaso kōzo, 10.5 g/m²), even across losses three inches wide, and then infilled with a mitsumata paper (Seikosen mitsumata, 40 g/m²) to match the thickness and colour of the original. The book was resewn and can again be opened fully.

sources.label: The Met Perspectives: Plant Bible Revival (Kramer, 2017)

facts.title: British Museum: a Ming painting on silk (relining)
facts.text: A Ming-dynasty painting on silk, 'Portrait of an official in front of the Beijing imperial palace' (c. 1480–1580, 1881,1210,0.87.CH; attributed to Zhu Bang in the blog, catalogued as anonymous), was remounted in the Hirayama Studio with traditional Chinese mounting techniques. The treatment included washing four times, removing the old lining fibre by fibre, and repairing silk losses with old silk. It was relined in two layers bonded with wheat starch paste: first a dyed Chinese xuan paper (short fibre), then a long-fibred Japanese usumino. A senior conservator of the Shanghai Museum took part in the lining stage. Washi here is the lining paper; the painting itself is on silk.

sources.label: British Museum blog: Bringing a Ming painting back to life
